entities.name: Cathal mac Finguine
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cathal mac Finguine, King of Munster from 721 CE until his death in 742 CE, emerged as one of the most powerful and ambitious rulers in early medieval Ireland, directly challenging the hegemonic aspirations of the Uí Néill dynasties. Ruling from Cashel, his reign marked a period of intense rivalry between the southern Eóganachta of Munster and the dominant northern and southern branches of the Uí Néill, shaping the political landscape of Ireland for decades. His strategic prowess and military campaigns cemented Munster's influence in the south-west and established a counterweight to the Uí Néill's claims of high-kingship.

Cathal's ascent to power was punctuated by significant military engagements, most notably the Battle of Cenn Abrat in 721 CE, where he consolidated his position within Munster by defeating the Eóganacht Glendamnach. His external policy was characterized by direct confrontation with the Uí Néill, culminating in the pivotal Battle of Knockroe (Cenn Corann) in 738 CE against Flaithbertach mac Loingsig, the Uí Néill High King. Although the annals record a defeat for Cathal in this engagement, his persistent challenge forced the Uí Néill to acknowledge Munster's formidable power and territorial integrity, preventing their complete dominance over the island.

His legacy endured through the continued strength of the Eóganachta and the enduring political structure of Munster, which remained a significant independent kingdom despite Uí Néill pressures. Cathal's reign solidified Munster's identity and contributed to the multi-polar political system of early medieval Ireland, where regional kingships fiercely guarded their autonomy. The patterns of inter-dynastic warfare and diplomatic maneuvering established during his time continued to define Irish politics until the Viking Age.
